title: Exploring the Indium phosphide supply chain — the material constraint tightening the optical interconnect bottleneck
summary: The AI industry's shift to optical interconnects is overwhelming the concentrated InP supply chain behind lasers, transceivers, and co-packaged optics.
body: Indium phosphide (InP) is a compound material used in specialized chip-making. Unlike silicon, which is the fundamental building block for mainstream logic and memory chips, InP — made from indium and phosphorus — is mainly used to manufacture highly specialized photonic and high-frequency electronic chips, largely due to its outstanding optical properties. Its immensely expensive and complex manufacturing process also makes it impractical for the large volumes and die sizes needed for logic and memory chips. With the industry predicting a shortfall of this crucial material right as the shift to optical interconnects in data centers begins, we explore the current state of the supply chain. InP chips have powered high-speed lasers, modulators, photodetectors, and various other optical components used across the telecommunications industry and defense for decades. While the InP supply chain was relatively small and highly specialized, it was generally stable and sufficient to meet global demands. Then came the AI boom. As AI clusters hit the physical limits of moving enormous amounts of data over copper, the industry began the switch to optical interconnects. First came ever-faster …

title: AI models on one vLLM server secretly talk through GPU rounding errors
summary: Two AI models on one vLLM inference server traded secret messages through GPU kernel rounding errors, with no network or shared files.
body: Sandboxed AI models on the same vLLM inference server can reliably exchange information even when cut off from the network and from any shared files, new research shows . Two models secretly communicated through tiny GPU rounding errors over two separate channels with perfect accuracy. In a follow-up experiment, a trained watchdog let all 354 of its partner’s attacks through while still catching most of the decoy honeypots, too. The research comes from a LessWrong post by Niranjan Deshpande and David Africa, “Models Can Communicate via Inference Servers Despite Being Sandboxed.” The agents primarily worked through two protocols, “Step Sizing” and “KV Cache Message Board,” to carry information through the way vLLM, an open-source inference engine , selects GPU kernels for each engine step. At the crux of it, one model modifies how the server batches work, and the other reads the traces in its own math, much like the OpenAI red-team agents that built a hidden CPU cache channel to talk last month. (Image credit: Niranjan Deshpande and David Africa/LessWrong ) The two demonstrations, which are shared in a GitHub repository, are “quite contrived,” but one model could affect another’s c…

summary: TSMC’s Texas filing describes a $22.6 billion project in Brazos County for 2nm or more advanced chips, starting production in 2031.
body: TSMC has made an application for a new fab and campus near College Station, Brazos County, Texas. The proposed fab would be just one county over from Terafab, would likely share supply chains, and would be positioned to make 2nm-class chips by 2031, with the $22.6 billion plan detailing how the Taiwanese chipmaker is planning to expand its U.S. operations. An application under Texas’s Jobs, Energy, Technology and Innovation (JETI) program for a school property-tax limit shows TSMC is weighing a new fab site. The fab wouldn’t make 2nm or more advanced chips until 2031, six years after 2nm volume production began in Taiwan. It would come with a school-tax break valued at around $354 million. This would be the company’s “second campus” for advanced chipmaking in the U.S. and the first outside Arizona. The Comptroller has recommended the tax application for approval, which the school district and the governor still have to grant. The application comes from TSMC Arizona Corporation, which is TSMC’s subsidiary located in Phoenix. title: 7 new Intel Nova Lake-S Core Ultra 4000-series CPUs detailed in new leak
summary: A number of new, unannounced Intel Core Ultra 4000-series chips have been detailed in a Nova Lake document, ahead of what is expected to be an official unveiling of the chips at a next-generation desktop chip event in Berlin, Germany, in February 2027.
body: A newly leaked document purportedly details no less than seven new Nova Lake-S desktop processors based on C1 stepping qualification samples, including 28-core models, three months before Intel is expected to officially take the wraps off them. The new leak, from VideoCardz , includes an Intel warning that clock speeds and performance may change before the final products are ready to be shipped. But given the fact that this rarely happens when dealing with qualification samples, it's believed that the chips will likely be released just as they are outlined in the document, if the leak is accurate. Of the seven chips that have been detailed, the top-of-the-line Core Ultra 9 4970K BFC will be the one of most interest. It will reportedly feature 28 cores comprising eight performance cores, 16 efficiency cores, and four low-power efficient cores. Its base efficiency core clock speed of 2.7 GHz is eclipsed by the 5.5 GHz boost speed its performance cores will reach, while 144 MB of L3 cache and a 125-watt power rating round out the main figures.
